section.title: Lawsuits Among Believers
section.sectionRationale: The proud, divided Corinthians were dragging one another before pagan courts, airing their disputes before unbelievers. Paul is astonished: the saints will one day judge the world and even angels, so they are surely competent to settle trivial matters among themselves. To have lawsuits at all is already a defeat; better to be wronged than to shame the church and the name of Christ. Paul then presses further, warning that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God, and reminding the Corinthians of the great reversal of the gospel: such were some of you, but you were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit.
section.thesis: Believers who take one another to court before unbelievers shame the church and are already defeated, for the saints will judge the world and angels and ought rather to be wronged than to sin against a brother; yet the deepest hope is that those once marked by such sins have been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the scandal of lawsuits before unbelievers, when the saints will judge the world and angels; the call rather to be wronged than to wrong a brother; and the sober warning that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom, answered by the gospel reversal, but you were washed, sanctified, justified.

units.label: Lawsuits before unbelievers
units.note: the saints will judge the world and angels

verses.text: If any of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the {{adikos|unrighteous}} instead of before the saints!
Do you not know that the saints will {{krino|judge}} the world? And if you are to judge the world, are you not competent to judge trivial cases?
Do you not know that we will judge angels? How much more the things of this life!
So if you need to settle everyday matters, do you appoint as judges those of no standing in the church?
I say this to your shame. Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers?
Instead, one brother goes to law against another, and this in front of unbelievers!

units.label: Better to be wronged
units.note: the lawsuits themselves are already a defeat

verses.text: The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means that you are thoroughly defeated already. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?
Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, even against your own brothers!

units.label: Washed, sanctified, justified
units.note: the unrighteous will not inherit, but such were some of you

verses.text: Do you not know that the wicked will not {{kleronomeo|inherit}} the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts,
nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God.
And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were {{dikaioo|justified}}, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.

adikos.gloss: Unrighteous, unjust, one who does not do what is right. Paul uses it for the pagan judges before whom the Corinthians were dragging their disputes, and it forms a pointed link with the unrighteous who will not inherit the kingdom in verse 9. It is folly to seek justice from the unrighteous when the saints themselves are destined to judge the world.

krino.gloss: To judge, to decide, to pass verdict. Paul reminds the saints of their astonishing future: they will judge the world and even angels alongside Christ. If such judgment awaits them, they are surely able to arbitrate the small everyday matters that divide them now, rather than parading their disputes before unbelieving courts.

kleronomeo.gloss: To inherit, to receive a share in an inheritance as an heir. The kingdom of God is an inheritance, received not earned, yet those who persist unrepentant in the works of the flesh show they have no part in it. The warning is solemn and real, and it sets up the glorious contrast of verse 11, that such people can be washed and made heirs.

dikaioo.gloss: To justify, to declare righteous, to acquit and count as right before God. Paul says the Corinthians, once marked by the sins that bar people from the kingdom, were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit. It is God's verdict of righteousness, grounded in Christ, that transfers them from the ranks of the unrighteous to the heirs of the kingdom.

basic.context: The Corinthians were suing one another in the pagan courts, letting unbelievers settle disputes between believers. Paul is amazed. Do they not know that one day the saints will judge the world, and even angels? If so, they can surely handle small everyday matters among themselves. In fact, having lawsuits at all is already a defeat; it would be better to accept being wronged than to shame Christ before outsiders. Yet instead they were the ones cheating their own brothers. Paul then warns that people who live in unrepentant sin will not inherit God's kingdom, and lists the very sins that describe the old life. But then comes the turn of the gospel: such were some of you. You were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul argues from the believers' future glory, judging the world and angels, back to their present pettiness. The vice list in verses 9 and 10 is a sober warning, not a cold catalogue; it exists to magnify the grace of verse 11. The threefold washed, sanctified, justified is the heart of the passage and must be read as the definitive answer to the warning.
basic.originalLanguages: It is folly to seek justice from the adikos, the unrighteous, when the saints will one day krino, judge, the world and angels. Paul warns that the unrighteous will not kleronomeo, inherit, the kingdom, an inheritance received by grace. Then the great reversal: the Corinthians were dikaioo, justified, declared righteous, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit.
basic.typology: The saints reigning and judging with Christ fulfil the promise that God's people would share in His rule, seen in the vision of the holy ones given judgment in Daniel and echoed in the reign of the saints in Revelation.
basic.christ: The transformation of the Corinthians happens in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ: His person and work are the ground of their washing, sanctifying, and justifying. Christ is the judge with whom the saints will judge the world, and it is union with Him, applied by the Spirit, that moves people from the list of the unrighteous to the heirs of the kingdom. The willingness to be wronged rather than retaliate reflects the pattern of Christ, who when reviled did not revile in return.
basic.god: God is just and will judge; the unrighteous will not inherit His kingdom. Yet God is the one who washes, sanctifies, and justifies sinners, taking the initiative to make the unrighteous righteous through Christ and by His Spirit. The kingdom is His to give as an inheritance, and He gives it freely to those who are His in Christ. His justice and His mercy are both fully in view.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 7 promises judgment given to the saints of the Most High. Revelation 20 shows the saints reigning and judging with Christ. Romans 12 urges believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's justice. Titus 3 describes the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Spirit.
basic.oneStory: God is forming a people who will share in His righteous rule, judging the world and angels with Christ. The petty lawsuits of Corinth deny that destiny. But the gospel reversal, washed, sanctified, justified, is the story of the whole Bible in miniature: God takes the unrighteous and makes them heirs of His kingdom through Christ and by the Spirit. The story runs from sinners barred from the kingdom to saints who will judge the world.

context.literary:
The section is a small essay in three panels, and each panel is hinged on the same phrase, 'Do you not know,' which Paul uses in verses 2, 3 and 9 and which recurs through chapters 5 and 6 as a refrain of rebuke. It is a polite way of saying that the Corinthians are behaving as if they had never been taught what they were taught. The first panel, verses 1 to 6, argues from the greater to the lesser: if the saints will sit in judgment on the world and on angels, then the 'trivial cases' of verse 2 and the 'everyday matters' of verse 4 are small things. The second, verses 7 and 8, turns from procedure to the heart and shows that the real fault lies in the wrongdoing, not the venue. The third, verses 9 to 11, turns again, from rebuke to warning to a burst of grace.

The passage is held together by one family of words. The 'unrighteous' of verse 1 are the adikoi, and the same word returns in verse 9, where the adikoi will not inherit the kingdom. In between, verses 7 and 8 use the matching verb twice, 'be wronged' and 'do wrong.' So the Corinthians go to the adikoi for justice while behaving as adikoi themselves, and verse 11 closes the circle: those who were adikoi have been 'justified,' made dikaioi. Paul also leaves a deliberate echo of chapter 5. There he told them to judge those inside the church and leave outsiders to God, 5:12-13. Here the same logic appears from the other side: they must not hand insiders to outsiders.

The tone changes sharply at verse 5, 'I say this to your shame,' and verse 5 ends with a question that has no answer in the church's favour, 'Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate?' Coming from a letter that has already mocked their claim to wisdom, 1:18 to 2:16, the irony is heavy.
context.historical:
Corinth was a Roman colony refounded in 44 BC, full of freedmen, traders and ambitious newcomers, and its public life ran on status. Civil disputes were heard before a magistrate and a panel, and the system leaned toward those with money, connections and rhetorical skill. A lawsuit was therefore less a quest for justice than a way for a wealthy person to humble a rival in public. The church at Corinth had a few such people, 1:26, and Paul's remark that the plaintiff is a 'brother' suing 'brothers' hints at the social direction of the suits: the stronger members were using the machinery against weaker ones, which fits verse 8, where it is the Corinthians who do the cheating.

Paul himself knew Corinth's tribunal. According to Acts 18:12-17 the Jews dragged him before the proconsul Gallio at the judgment seat, and Gallio drove them off, refusing to be a judge of disputes about their own law. The Corinthian believers had therefore seen at close range how little interest a pagan magistrate had in matters of faith.

Paul's own background also matters. Jewish communities scattered through the empire were used to settling their disputes among themselves, and the church inherited that instinct, which is why 'arbitrate' in verse 5 is the natural word. The phrase 'those of no standing in the church' in verse 4 is probably sharp irony. The word is the one Paul used in 1:28 for the despised and lowly whom God chose, so if the world's courts count for nothing in God's eyes, why would the church treat them as authorities?

The vice list that follows is the sort of catalogue common in Greek moral writing, but here it is not a general sermon. It describes the city around them and, as verse 11 says, the people they used to be.
context.canonical:
The promise that the saints will judge begins in Daniel 7, where the Ancient of Days 'pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High,' Daniel 7:22, and the kingdom is given to them. Jesus carried the theme forward when He told the Twelve that they would sit on thrones 'judging the twelve tribes of Israel,' Luke 22:30, and Matthew 19:28 places that in 'the renewal of all things.' Revelation 20:4 pictures thrones and 'those seated on them had been given authority to judge.' Paul's 'do you not know' suggests that he had already taught this to the Corinthians as settled apostolic instruction.

The judging of angels connects to two New Testament texts about angels held for judgment, 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6, and it is natural to read Paul as saying that believers will share in Christ's verdict over fallen powers. How that sharing works is not explained, and the text gives no further detail.

The call to accept wrong instead of retaliating belongs to the heart of Jesus' teaching. Matthew 5:40 pictures someone wanting to sue for your tunic and being given the cloak as well, and Romans 12:17-21 forbids repaying evil for evil. The pattern is finally Christ's own, who 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23.

The vice list has close relatives in Galatians 5:19-21, which ends with the same warning about not inheriting the kingdom, and 1 Timothy 1:9-10. The closing verse, with its triple 'you were,' draws on the language of Titus 3:5, 'the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,' and of Ephesians 5:26. Together they show that Paul is drawing on a stock of baptismal language the early church shared.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Corinthians to feel the contradiction. They think of themselves as wise, spiritual and rich, 4:8, yet they are asking pagans to decide among them, and in doing so they tell the city that the church cannot manage its own household. He does not give them a rule of procedure. He gives them an identity: you are the people who will judge the world, so act like it. The argument works from destiny to present behaviour.

He also wants them to see that the lawsuits are a symptom. Verse 7 says the defeat has already happened, whoever wins the case, because a brother has been treated as an opponent. The deeper issue is the wrong done, and verse 8 turns the finger back on the plaintiffs themselves. Paul expects the hearers to flinch.

The last paragraph is not meant to frighten them out of the faith. 'Do not be deceived' shows that some were assuming their conduct did not matter, but the list ends in grace. His purpose is that the church would remember what it was, what it has become, and by whose name and Spirit it was made new, and that this memory would cut the root of their litigiousness and their sexual and financial greed together.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a real situation, believers suing one another in Roman courts, and Paul prescribes a response: settle matters inside the church, using a wise arbitrator, and prefer suffering loss to damaging a brother or the gospel's reputation. He does not address criminal acts, such as violence or abuse, and he is not saying that the church replaces the state, which Romans 13:1-4 treats as God's servant for justice. Paul himself appealed to Caesar when he was wrongly held, Acts 25:11. So the principle is aimed at disputes between believers that the church is able to hear, not at every legal question or at serious crime.

The vice list is description, not an exhaustive code, and verse 11 is also description: 'that is what some of you were.' Treating verse 9 as a verdict on any person who struggles with one of these sins reads past verse 11. The warning applies to settled, unrepentant patterns of life, and the promise of washing applies to every believer who has turned to Christ. A church that follows Paul will name sin honestly and receive sinners warmly, and it will not treat any one category of sin as worse than the greed and drunkenness listed beside it.

debates.question: What does it mean that the saints will judge the world and angels?

views.label: Sharing in Christ's final verdict
views.case: Daniel 7:22 gives judgment to the saints, Luke 22:30 promises thrones, and Revelation 20:4 pictures those who sit on them with authority to judge. On this reading believers will take part in the last judgment, assenting to and participating in Christ's rule over the nations and over fallen angels, whom Peter and Jude describe as held for judgment, 2 Peter 2:4, Jude 6.

views.label: Ruling with Christ in the age to come
views.case: The Greek verb for judging can mean governing as well as condemning, as it does in the book of Judges. Paul's point would then be that the saints are destined to reign, so they are certainly fit to govern small disputes now. This view stresses the continuity with Jesus' promise to the Twelve and with Revelation's reigning saints.

debates.bearing: Both views share Paul's logic. His argument needs only the conviction that believers are destined to share in Christ's rule, so that settling a quarrel over property is beneath their calling, not above their ability.

debates.question: Does Paul forbid every Christian from going to law?

views.label: No lawsuits between believers at all
views.case: Verse 7 says the very fact of lawsuits is already a defeat and recommends being wronged. Taken at face value, believers should absorb loss and not bring cases against one another, and the church should provide arbitration.

views.label: Not before unbelievers over matters the church can judge
views.case: Paul's rebuke is aimed at suing 'before the unrighteous instead of before the saints,' verse 1, and at the shame of unbelievers watching, verse 6. He himself used Roman legal rights, Acts 25:11, and Romans 13:1-4 honours the state's role. Disputes beyond the church's competence, and crimes against the vulnerable, are therefore a different matter.

debates.bearing: Everyone agrees that the church should have a way of settling disputes among believers and that the first instinct should be to forgive or absorb the loss, Matthew 18:15-17. The disagreement is whether any civil action remains open as a last resort, and that depends on how far one reads Paul's example in Acts 25 as binding.

debates.question: How should the vice list of verses 9 and 10, including its words about sexual sin, be understood and applied?

views.label: A sober warning against unrepentant sin
views.case: The list names patterns of settled, unrepentant behaviour that mark the life of those outside the kingdom; it warns professing believers not to be deceived into thinking such a life is compatible with inheriting the kingdom, while treating all the sins named, from greed and drunkenness to sexual sin, with equal seriousness.

views.label: A backdrop for grace, not a verdict of no hope
views.case: The whole point of the list is verse 11, such were some of you: these very sins do not place anyone beyond the reach of Christ, for the Corinthians themselves were washed, sanctified, and justified; the passage offers real hope and transformation, not condemnation without remedy.

debates.bearing: Read together, the two views guard both truth and grace: sin must be named honestly and not excused, yet no sinner who turns to Christ is beyond washing and justification; the passage is pastoral and hopeful, never a license to despair or to condemn.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's Greek has a rhythm that English loses. In verse 1 the verb 'dare' is tolmao, the word for nerve and brazenness, and it opens the section with a sneer: how can anyone have the nerve? The 'trivial cases' of verse 2 are literally 'smallest courts' or criteria, the court as the place where decisions are made. Verse 4 uses a related word for 'everyday matters,' pertaining to biotika, life, as opposed to the final things. Paul sets the whole of daily life against the whole of the age to come.

The phrase 'those of no standing' in verse 4 comes from exoutheneo, to treat as nothing. It is the same word family Paul used in 1:28 for the 'lowly and despised things' that God chose. The irony is that the church's judges, whom the Corinthians despise, are the very kind of people God delights to use, while the world's judges are the ones counted as nothing.

In verse 5 'arbitrate' is diakrino, 'to decide between,' a compound of the krino of verse 2, and the verb of discernment elsewhere in the letter. Verse 7 gives 'defeat' as hettema, a rare noun for a loss, failure or diminishing. Romans 11:12 uses it of Israel's 'failure.' The Corinthians think they win by winning cases; Paul says the loss is already counted.

The two verbs of verse 7 and 8 are adikeo, 'be wronged,' and apostereo, 'cheat' or defraud, 'strip.' Paul uses apostereo again in 7:5, 'do not deprive each other,' so the same verb names defrauding a brother in property and defrauding a spouse in marriage. In both cases the wrong is taking from a person what is owed.

Verse 9 says 'do not be deceived,' me planasthe, a phrase that Paul uses elsewhere to cut off self-excuse, as in 15:33. The vice list pairs two words that the BSB renders 'men who submit to or perform homosexual acts.' The second, arsenokoites, is a compound of the words for male and bed, and readers often note that it echoes the Septuagint wording of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13. The first, malakos, literally 'soft,' is debated, and translators differ on how it should be rendered. The BSB's choice reads the two as a pair.

Verse 11 is built on three aorist verbs, 'you washed,' 'you were sanctified,' 'you were justified,' joined to the opening 'but,' repeated three times in the Greek, a stuttering emphasis. The first verb, apelousasthe, is in the middle voice: you washed yourselves, or had yourselves washed. Acts 22:16 uses the same verb for Ananias telling Paul to 'wash your sins away,' calling on the name. The other two verbs are passive, as God is the actor in making holy and declaring righteous. The verbs do not follow a neat order. Sanctified comes before justified, a reminder that Paul is not laying out a ladder but piling up three descriptions of one event.

The last phrase has two parts, 'in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ' and 'by the Spirit of our God,' giving the Son as the sphere and the Spirit as the agent of the whole change.

typology.type: The holy ones who receive judgment, Daniel 7:22
typology.fulfillment: In Daniel's vision the Ancient of Days gives judgment in favour of 'the saints of the Most High' and they possess the kingdom. Paul assumes the Corinthians already know that this describes them. Jesus prepared the way by promising the Twelve thrones, Luke 22:30, and Revelation 20:4 sees the thrones filled. The correspondence rises from a persecuted remnant being vindicated to ordinary believers in a quarrelsome Greek city being told that their destiny is to judge. The type falls short in one respect: the saints judge only as they share in Christ, the Son of Man who holds all judgment.

Aaron and his sons were washed with water at the door of the tent before they could serve, a washing that marked them as set apart. Paul's 'you were washed' takes that picture and applies it to every believer, with Titus 3:5 speaking of 'the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit' and Ephesians 5:26 of Christ cleansing His church. Hebrews 10:22 speaks of bodies 'washed with pure water.' The escalation is from a ritual that had to be repeated to a cleansing the Spirit completes once, and from a priestly family to a whole people.

typology.type: The wronged one who does not retaliate, Isaiah 53:7
typology.fulfillment: The Servant is oppressed and afflicted yet 'did not open His mouth,' and the New Testament sees Jesus in this figure, Acts 8:32-35. Peter applies it to the way Christ behaved when abused: He 'did not retaliate,' but entrusted Himself to the just Judge, 1 Peter 2:23. Paul's counsel to be wronged is not a general ethic of passivity but a call to follow the pattern. The correspondence falls short because the Servant's suffering was also atoning, and a believer's patience under wrong is never that.

typology.type: The land that is received, not earned, Hebrews 11:8
typology.fulfillment: Abraham went out to a place that he would later receive as an inheritance, and Israel's land was given by promise, not by conquest alone. Paul's talk of inheriting the kingdom takes that pattern and makes it the goal of the whole redeemed people. The warning of verses 9 and 10 is the same warning given to Israel in the wilderness, which Paul will spell out in 10:1-12: privilege does not guard against falling. The type finds its fulfilment when the kingdom is not a strip of land but the renewed creation, Revelation 21:1.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most plainly in the phrase 'in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ,' verse 11. The name stands for His person and authority and, in the Corinthian setting, probably recalls the confession and baptism in which the new life began, Acts 22:16. Everything that is true of the reformed Corinthians is said to be true in Him. Paul says elsewhere that Christ became for us 'wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption,' 1 Corinthians 1:30. Verse 11 uses two of the same words, 'justified' and 'sanctified,' and the same logic: righteousness and holiness are not qualities the Corinthians achieved but gifts of the person to whom they belong.

It leads to Christ as the Judge with whom the saints will judge. The authority is His. Daniel's 'one like a son of man' is given dominion and the kingdom, Daniel 7:13-14, and the saints receive it with Him. Paul's argument is therefore not that Christians are wise lawyers in waiting but that they will share in the rule of the One who has already been raised to the right hand of God. A community that will govern the world beside Him is being ridiculous when it hands a petty case to a magistrate who does not know Him.

It leads to Christ by pattern. 'Why not rather be wronged?' is not a new demand. Isaiah's Servant 'did not open His mouth,' Isaiah 53:7, and Peter says that when Jesus was abused 'He did not retaliate,' but entrusted Himself to the Judge who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. The Lord who could call down judgment accepted the verdict of a pagan court, and by accepting it He won the only acquittal that will ever stand. Paul's ethic of absorbing loss is a way of showing the cross to the watching world.

It leads to Christ by the exchange the gospel makes. 'Such were some of you' acknowledges a real past, and 'but you were justified' points to a real transfer: the unrighteous are declared righteous because the Righteous One took their place, 2 Corinthians 5:21. Titus 3:5 insists that this happens 'not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy.' The inheritance of verse 9 is therefore not something the unrighteous fail to earn and the righteous earn; it is something the unrighteous are given when they are joined to Christ.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Paul does not say that the washing removes the temptation or that the Corinthians no longer sin, as the rest of the letter shows. He says that the status and the power belong to them now, and that this is the ground for the lives he is asking them to live.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who is both just and merciful, and who refuses to let either side swallow the other. He will judge: the world and angels will stand before the saints because they stand before Him, and the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom. The words are blunt, and Paul adds 'do not be deceived' because it is possible to be convinced that a holy God does not mind. Yet the one who judges is also the one who washes. The verbs of verse 11 are passive for sanctifying and justifying, so God is the agent: He makes holy, He declares righteous, and the Spirit applies it. Nothing in the list of sins puts a person beyond His reach, and nothing in the washing excuses a return to those sins.

The passage also shows how God relates to His people's honour. He assigns the saints a future role in judgment, trusting them with authority as a father gives a son responsibility. That is why the Corinthians' behaviour grieves Him: they are acting beneath the dignity He has given them. At the same time, He cares about the reputation of His name before unbelievers who are watching, verse 6. Quarrelling believers misrepresent Him, and He is jealous that the world should see in His church a community that looks like Him.

Here the Trinity is quietly present. The Lord Jesus Christ supplies the name and the ground, the Spirit supplies the power, and 'our God' is the source of the whole change. The doctrine is not argued but assumed, and it lies behind everything Paul says about being washed and justified.

The tension between 'will not inherit' and 'you were justified' is real but not contradictory. The first speaks to those who think they can persist in unrepentant wrongdoing and still count on the kingdom. The second speaks to those who have turned and been made new. God's justice is the reason the warning is true, and His mercy is the reason the remedy is real.

For worship this means two things. We honour a God before whom believers are given trust and also called to account, and so we can neither presume nor despair. And we worship a God whose way with the wronged is not retaliation but patient justice. A church that has been washed by Him has every reason to prefer losing a case to losing a brother.

crossReferences.note: The Ancient of Days gives judgment in favour of the saints, and the time comes for them to possess the kingdom. This is the background to Paul's 'Do you not know that the saints will judge the world?' and shows that his argument rests on a promise the church already had.

Jesus promises the apostles that they will eat at His table in His kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes. The authority to judge belongs to those who share His kingdom, which grounds Paul's claim that the Corinthians are fit for even small matters.

Just before this passage Paul says that he has no business judging outsiders, since God will judge them, but that the church is to judge those inside. Chapter 6 shows the reverse failure: the church hands its own cases to outsiders. The two passages belong together.

Jesus gives the church its own process for a brother who sins: private conversation, then witnesses, then the church. Paul's call to arbitration within the church puts this pattern into practice and shows why a pagan court is not the first, or even a fit, place for such disputes.

Jesus pictures a person who wants to sue for your tunic and is given the cloak as well. Paul's 'Why not rather be wronged?' is the same ethic applied to a real legal situation, and Jesus' example shows that giving up a claim can be a way of overcoming evil.

Paul tells the Romans not to repay evil for evil and to leave room for God's wrath, 'Vengeance is Mine.' The idea behind 1 Corinthians 6:7 is the same: believers can absorb a loss because they trust that God is the final judge and will set things right.

When Christ was abused He did not retaliate but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. This is the model behind Paul's counsel. The Judge of the whole earth can be trusted, so the one wronged can afford to be patient.

A parallel list of the acts of the flesh that ends with the same warning that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. Reading the two together shows that Paul uses lists of this kind as a pastoral warning, not as a way to rank people.

God saved us 'not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.' This is the same grace-centred language as 'you were washed' and shows that the Corinthian verse is a summary of a shared apostolic message.

Ananias tells Paul, 'Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.' The verb is the one Paul uses in verse 11, and 'calling on His name' matches 'in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.' It suggests that Paul has the Corinthians' conversion in mind.

Paul himself was once brought before the judgment seat in Corinth, and the proconsul Gallio refused to judge a dispute about religious matters. The Corinthians knew from experience that pagan magistrates had no interest in the questions that mattered most to believers.

Christ Jesus 'has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption.' Two of these gifts, righteousness and holiness, are the ones named in 6:11, and the earlier verse explains why: they come with being in Christ, not from the believer's own record.

study.oneStory:
The question this passage answers is what a redeemed people is for. From the first chapters of Genesis, humans were made to rule under God, to 'fill the earth and subdue it,' Genesis 1:28, and to judge rightly, as the garden's test of wisdom shows, Genesis 2:16-17. The fall corrupted rule into rivalry and judgment into accusation. By Genesis 4 a brother's blood is crying out from the ground, and quarrels over land and wells and wives run through the patriarchal stories. Israel, set apart as a kingdom of priests, was given judges and a law to settle disputes, and the prophets repeatedly show how corrupt courts became, Isaiah 1:23.

The passage sets up the end of the story. Daniel saw the kingdom given to the saints of the Most High, and Paul reminds the Corinthians that this is their destiny. Redemption is not only forgiveness for the past but a restoration of the human calling to rule. Revelation 20:4 sees the thrones filled with those who 'reigned with Christ,' and the new creation is a place where the Lamb's people serve and reign forever, Revelation 22:5.

Between the fall and the new creation, the church is meant to be a foretaste. A community that settles its disputes by confession, reconciliation and, where needed, wise arbitration, is a small picture of the world to come. A community that drags itself into court is a picture of the old world, still caught in the quarrels of Genesis 4. That is why Paul takes the lawsuits so seriously.

Verse 11 is the hinge of the larger story in miniature. The Corinthians were the people Paul describes in the list, and they are now the washed, the sanctified and the justified. The same God who drove the first humans from the garden has made a way for unrighteous people to be declared righteous and to enter an inheritance. The warning that the unrighteous will not inherit and the promise that they have been justified are two halves of the same plot, and the Bible's final page, where nothing unclean enters the city but the washed enter freely, Revelation 22:14, is where it resolves.

quiz.q: Why is Paul astonished that the Corinthians take their disputes to pagan courts?

options.text: Because the saints will one day judge the world and even angels.
options.note: Verses 2 and 3 ground the rebuke in the saints' future role as judges.

options.text: Because pagan courts always ruled unfairly.
options.note: Bias was real, but Paul's argument is the saints' own destiny to judge.

options.text: Because lawsuits were illegal for believers.
options.note: The issue is not legality but the shame and inconsistency of it.

options.text: Because Christians should never resolve disputes at all.
options.note: Paul wants disputes settled, but within the church, by the wise.

quiz.q: What does Paul say the lawsuits themselves already reveal?

options.text: That the Corinthians are thoroughly defeated already.
options.note: Verse 7 says having lawsuits at all is already a defeat.

options.text: That they simply need better lawyers.
options.note: The problem is spiritual defeat, not legal strategy.

options.text: That they are zealous for justice.
options.note: Their zeal is misdirected; the lawsuits are a failure, not a virtue.

options.text: That the church is spiritually healthy.
options.note: The lawsuits are a symptom of deep dysfunction.

quiz.q: What does Paul urge as better than suing a brother?

options.text: To rather be wronged or cheated than to shame the church.
options.note: Verse 7 asks, why not rather be wronged, why not rather be cheated.

options.text: To retaliate quietly outside the courts.
options.note: Retaliation is not the answer; Paul counsels willingness to suffer wrong.

options.text: To ignore all wrongdoing as if it did not happen.
options.note: The point is not indifference but willingness to bear loss for Christ.

options.text: To demand full repayment before forgiving.
options.note: This is the opposite of being willing to be wronged.

quiz.q: What sober warning does Paul give in verses 9 and 10?

options.text: The unrighteous who persist unrepentant will not inherit the kingdom of God.
options.note: Verses 9 and 10 warn that such a life excludes from the kingdom.

options.text: That some sins are too small for God to notice.
options.note: Paul takes every sin named seriously, not lightly.

options.text: That believers can sin freely without consequence.
options.note: The warning is precisely against presuming on grace.

options.text: That no one can ever be sure of the kingdom.
options.note: Verse 11 gives real assurance to those washed and justified.

quiz.q: What is the gospel reversal Paul declares in verse 11?

options.text: Such were some of you, but you were washed, sanctified, and justified in Christ and by the Spirit.
options.note: Verse 11 is the triumphant turn from the vice list to grace.

options.text: That they cleaned up their own lives by effort.
options.note: The change is God's work in Christ and by the Spirit, not self-reform.

options.text: That their past sins still define them.
options.note: Paul says such were some of you, past tense; they have been changed.

options.text: That only some of the sins could be forgiven.
options.note: The whole list is answered by the washing and justifying grace of God.

questions: Paul says the saints will judge the world and angels. How might remembering your eternal destiny reshape the way you handle a present conflict?
Better to be wronged than to shame Christ before outsiders. Is there a dispute where you are being called to absorb loss rather than fight to win?
The lawsuits themselves were already a defeat. Where might winning an argument actually mean losing something far more important?
The vice list describes a life outside the kingdom, yet such were some of you. How does that phrase give you hope for yourself or for someone you have given up on?
You were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit. Which of those three words do you most need to hear over your life today?
Paul assumes the church should be able to resolve its own disputes wisely. What would it take for your community to become a place where that is true?

translationNotes.note: Before the unrighteous renders the same root, adikos, used in verse 9 for those who will not inherit the kingdom; Paul highlights the irony of seeking justice from the unrighteous.

The phrase rendered men who submit to or perform homosexual acts translates two Greek terms describing both partners in male same-sex activity; the list treats this sin alongside greed, theft, and drunkenness, all named with equal seriousness and all answered by the grace of verse 11.

Washed, sanctified, justified are three complementary pictures of one saving work, done in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God, and are best read as God's decisive act, not a gradual self-improvement.
